extracted.intended_audience: literature students, Melville scholars, and general readers of literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Close-read and evaluate Herman Melville's Moby-Dick with attention to style, imagery, influences, composition process, and publication/contextual factors that shaped the novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similes' imaginative abundance
rubrics_metrics.description: These similes, with their astonishing 'imaginative abundance,' not only create dramatic movement ... notable for breadth; and the more sustained among them, for an heroic dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similes should be sustained and broad in scope to produce dramatic movement and heroic dignity; examples cited include imagery that fuses crew and ship into oneness and mastheads 'outspreadingly tufted with arms and legs.' Avoid thin or purely decorative comparisons that fail to contribute to narrative propulsion or thematic unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagery that concentrates narrative energy and dwarfs everything but the protagonist's will
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagery serves to dwarf everything but Ahab's will in the presence of Moby Dick; images contribute their 'startling energy' to the advance of the narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use accumulative, high-energy images to focus reader attention on the central will or conflict; imagery should both amplify action and subordinate secondary elements to the protagonist's drive. Anti-pattern: imagery that disperses focus or competes with the central motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assimilation of Shakespearean resources without imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Melville's 'possession by Shakespeare' made him discover his own full strength ... the diction 'that depended upon no source' — language that suggests Shakespeare's but is not an imitation of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn from a major influence (e.g., Shakespeare) to enrich voice and dramatic technique, but transform rather than copy: adopt rhythm, dramatic diction, and imaginative breadth while creating original combinations of words and usages. Examples: melodic dramatic lines, echoing blanks of blank verse, but with fresh word combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading as catalytic agent (use reading/annotation to transform writing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading Shakespeare ... was 'a catalytic agent' that transformed his writing 'from limited reporting to the expression of profound natural forces.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deep immersion and annotation of model texts can catalyze a writer's transition from mere reportage to expressive, forceful prose. Practical guidance: study close examples (e.g., King Lear, Macbeth) and let elements of technique (rhythm, character construction) influence reworking of your own material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character creation by exaggerating a single faculty (Coleridge's mode)
rubrics_metrics.description: One of Shakespeare's modes of creating characters is to conceive any one intellectual or moral faculty in morbid excess ... thus mutilated or diseased, under given circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To create a tragic or memorable character, consider intensifying one trait to near-excess so it dominates motivation and action (Melville's Ahab as 'morbidness' in excess). Use this carefully to yield coherent tragic logic rather than caricature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make language itself dramatic (speech rhythm and verb-driven diction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Melville 'now mastered Shakespeare's mature secret of how to make language itself dramatic' ... to rely on verbs of action, 'which lend their dynamic pressure to both movement and meaning.' The prose is based on 'a sense of speech rhythm.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize active verbs and a spoken rhythmic cadence in prose to generate dramatic force. Techniques: favor verbs of action over nominalizations, craft sentences with breath-like cadence (as in dramatic speech), and consider how syntax contributes to immediacy. Anti-patterns: passive constructions and flattened diction that dissipate dramatic urgency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of verbal compounds and creative coinages for energy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Shakespearean energy of verbal compounds was not lost on him ('full-freighted'). ... making one part of speech act as another — for example, 'earthquake' as an adjective, or the coining of 'placeless'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ compounds, neologisms, and morphosyntactic shifts (noun to adjective, etc.) to quicken language and convey fresh perception. Balance novelty with intelligibility; avoid gratuitous coinages that obscure meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt philosophical/ rhetorical sources (e.g., Carlyle) to shape voice and narrative strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Carlyle's rhetoric is reflected in dialogue of Ahab and Ishmael; Melville uses Sartor's philosophical concepts of 'an emblematic universe' and a 'weaver god' and borrows narrative strategy and romantic ironic paradoxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate philosophical or rhetorical frameworks from other writers to inform narrative strategy, character portraiture, and ironic modes. Use such borrowings to generate thematic depth and distinctive rhetorical voice rather than mere pastiche.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate Renaissance humanist skepticism and epistemological paradox
rubrics_metrics.description: Melville adopted not only their poetic and conversational prose styles, but also their skeptical attitudes towards religion ... Ishmael embraces paradox: 'Doubts of all things earthly, and intuitions of some things heavenly ... makes neither believer nor infidel.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weave skeptical, paradox-friendly perspectives into narrator voice and thematic framing to achieve intellectual complexity. Use paradox as a deliberate stance rather than accidental inconsistency; it should clarify a worldview rather than simply confuse readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use encyclopedic and sonorous reference works as conceptual touchstones
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholars note Melville had Burton's Anatomy of Melancholy at his side; it served as a 'conceptual touchstone' and 'sonorous textbook on morbid psychology.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult encyclopedic or compendious works to supply tone, topical breadth, and conceptual apparatus; their diction and structures can inform chapter organization and thematic encyclopedism. Be prepared to adapt prosaic material into figurative, rhetorical prose for artistic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance factual source material with artistic adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: Melville followed Beale's grouping closely, yet adapted it to what art demanded, and he changed the original's prosaic phrases into graphic figures of speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using documentary or technical sources, let them shape factual arrangement and authenticity but transform their language and selection to serve aesthetic and thematic aims. Avoid slavish transcription of dry material; instead, reinterpret and dramatize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirize or invert dry source material to avoid dryness
rubrics_metrics.description: Melville satirized and parodied Scoresby's dryness and abundance of irrelevant data ... gave his account 'a humorous twist of fact.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If source materials are arid or overly factual, use satire, parody, or comic recontextualization to make them serve narrative and tonal purposes. This protects against boring, encyclopedic flatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use autobiographical experience selectively, not as literal autobiography
rubrics_metrics.description: Moby-Dick draws on Melville's experience on the whaler Acushnet, but is not autobiographical ... Melville meant to give the truth of the thing, spite of this (balancing fact and fancy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mine personal experience for authentic detail and incident but rework, fictionalize, and mythologize it to meet artistic aims. The goal is truthful effect rather than documentary fidelity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow composition to evolve through stages and external influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholars have concluded that Melville composed Moby-Dick in two or even three stages ... reading Shakespeare and friendship with Hawthorne inspired Melville to rewrite a 'relatively straightforward' whaling adventure into an epic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open to major revisions mid-project as new readings, friendships, or intellectual encounters change ambition and scope. Treat composition as potentially iterative and transformative rather than fixed from the outset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate editorial/printer constraints when revising
rubrics_metrics.description: While revising, earlier chapters were already plated when he was revising the later ones, so Melville 'must have felt restricted in the kinds of revisions that were feasible.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand production timelines (proofs, plating, typesetting) and how they limit late revisions; plan revision phases accordingly. Practical advice: schedule major structural changes before pages are plated or sent to external printers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select titles and dedications with commercial and rhetorical considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Melville changed the title to Moby-Dick late in the process — 'It is thought here that the new title will be a better selling title.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a title and dedication with an ear to both thematic resonance and marketability; last-minute title changes for selling appeal are a legitimate part of publication strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of contemporary censorship standards and probable grounds for expurgation
rubrics_metrics.description: British censorship expurgations fell into categories: sacrilegious passages (attributing human failures to God), sexual matters (sex life of whales, allusions to fornication), remarks belittling royalty, and perceived grammatical/stylistic anomalies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing a work for publication in conservative jurisdictions or periods, anticipate categories likely to be censored (religious offense, sexual explicitness, political insult, 'incorrect' grammar) and decide whether to preemptively revise, provide alternate editions, or risk excisions. Examples include the British edition's deletions and stylistic 'corrections.'
